questions.title: Fracture site affecting peroneus brevis insertion
questions.question: Fracture of which of the following bones will affect the insertion of the peroneus brevis muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The calcaneus receives the tendo calcaneus and long plantar ligament, not peroneus brevis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The navicular receives part of tibialis posterior's insertion, not peroneus brevis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The base of the first metatarsal (with the medial cuneiform) is where peroneus longus, not brevis, inserts.
explanations.D: Correct. Peroneus brevis inserts on the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal, so a fracture there (a "Jones fracture" in clinical shorthand) directly threatens this tendon's insertion. No other tarsal or metatarsal named in this stem carries peroneus brevis's insertion, which is what makes the fifth metatarsal base the single correct site.

questions.learning_objective: State that peroneus brevis inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal.

questions.title: The incorrect statement about leg muscles
questions.question: Regarding the muscles of the leg, the INCORRECT statement is:

options.A: Peroneus longus muscle is inserted into 5th metatarsal bone
options.B: The tibialis anterior is inserted into the medial cuneiform bone
options.C: The gastrocnemius is inserted into the back of calcaneus
options.D: The tibialis posterior is inserted into the tuberosity of the navicular bone

explanations.A: Correct — this is the incorrect (false) statement. Peroneus longus inserts on the base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform, not the fifth metatarsal; the fifth metatarsal is peroneus brevis's insertion. Recognising this reversed pairing — longus to the first metatarsal, brevis to the fifth — is the exact discrimination this stem tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement IS true). Tibialis anterior does insert on the medial cuneiform (and base of the first metatarsal).
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement IS true). Gastrocnemius, via the tendo calcaneus, does insert on the back of the calcaneus.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement IS true). Tibialis posterior's chief insertion is the tuberosity of the navicular, with slips to neighbouring tarsals.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that peroneus longus, not peroneus brevis, is the muscle whose fifth-metatarsal insertion is being misstated.

questions.title: The muscle that everts the foot
questions.question: Which of the following muscles everts the foot?

explanations.A: Correct. Peroneus longus, a lateral compartment muscle supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve, is a prime evertor of the foot, alongside peroneus brevis. Peroneus brevis, its close partner in the lateral compartment, shares this same eversion action and nerve supply.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Extensor hallucis longus dorsiflexes the ankle and extends the great toe; it has no eversion action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts, the opposite of eversion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Soleus plantarflexes the ankle and has no eversion action.

questions.learning_objective: Identify peroneus longus as a prime evertor of the foot.

questions.title: Nerve supply of peroneus brevis
questions.question: Peroneus brevis muscle is supplied by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The deep peroneal nerve supplies the anterior compartment (dorsiflexors), not the lateral compartment.
explanations.B: Correct. Peroneus brevis, like peroneus longus, is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve — termed the "musculocutaneous nerve of the leg" in this bank's older terminology. Recognising this older naming convention prevents a student from mistaking "musculocutaneous nerve" here for the upper-limb nerve of the same name, which is an entirely different structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The medial popliteal (tibial) nerve supplies the posterior compartment, not the lateral compartment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lateral plantar nerve supplies intrinsic sole muscles in the foot, an entirely different region from the leg's lateral compartment.

questions.learning_objective: Confirm that the superficial peroneal nerve (this bank's "musculocutaneous nerve of the leg") supplies peroneus brevis.

questions.title: Attachment of peroneus longus
questions.question: Peroneus longus muscle is attached to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The navicular receives part of tibialis posterior's insertion, not peroneus longus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cuboid only grooves peroneus longus's tendon as it crosses the sole; it is not the insertion point.
explanations.C: Correct. Peroneus longus's tendon crosses the sole obliquely to insert on the base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform. This insertion, shared with tibialis anterior at the same two bones from the opposite side of the foot, forms a functional "stirrup" that helps support the transverse arch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fifth metatarsal is peroneus brevis's insertion, not peroneus longus's.

questions.learning_objective: State that peroneus longus inserts on the base of the first metatarsal/medial cuneiform, not the fifth metatarsal.

questions.title: Structure at the neck of the fibula
questions.question: The neck of the fibula is related to:

explanations.A: Correct. The common peroneal nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula before dividing into its superficial and deep branches, making it directly vulnerable to fracture or external compression at that point. This superficial, subcutaneous position at the fibular neck is precisely why the nerve is also vulnerable to prolonged external pressure, such as from tight leg-crossing or a poorly padded cast.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral plantar nerve is a sole-of-foot structure, unrelated to the fibular neck.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The medial popliteal (tibial) nerve runs deep in the posterior compartment, well away from the subcutaneous fibular neck.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior tibial nerve likewise runs deep posteriorly, not at the fibular neck.

questions.learning_objective: State that the common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck, making it vulnerable there.

questions.title: Nerve damaged by a fibular neck fracture
questions.question: A 20-year-old college student receives a severe blow to the inferolateral side of the left knee joint while playing football. Radiographic examination reveals a fracture of the head and neck of the fibula. Which of the following nerves is damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sciatic nerve has already divided well above the knee in most people, so a fibular-neck fracture affects only its common peroneal branch, not the intact sciatic trunk.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tibial nerve runs deep in the posterior compartment, well away from the subcutaneous fibular neck.
explanations.C: Correct. The common peroneal nerve winds directly around the fibular neck, making it the nerve classically injured by a fracture at exactly this site. This mechanism — a direct blow or fracture compressing the nerve against the bone at its most exposed point — is the classic teaching example of a peripheral nerve injury from local trauma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The deep peroneal nerve is only the common peroneal nerve's distal branch, given off after it has already passed the fibular neck — the injury at the neck itself affects the whole common peroneal trunk, which is the more precise answer here.

questions.learning_objective: Localise a fibular neck fracture's nerve injury to the common peroneal nerve specifically.

questions.title: Muscle paralysed after the same injury
questions.question: After injury to this nerve (from the fibular neck fracture case), which muscle could be paralysed?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gastrocnemius is tibial-nerve-supplied, part of the uninjured posterior compartment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Popliteus is also tibial-nerve-supplied and would be spared.
explanations.C: Correct. Extensor hallucis longus is an anterior compartment muscle supplied by the deep peroneal branch of the common peroneal nerve, so it is paralysed by this injury. Because it is one of several deep peroneal-supplied muscles, extensor hallucis longus weakness is only part of the broader anterior-compartment foot-drop picture from this injury.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum longus is tibial-nerve-supplied and would be spared.

questions.learning_objective: Identify extensor hallucis longus as an anterior-compartment muscle paralysed by a common peroneal nerve injury.

questions.title: Nerve affected by a fibular neck fracture (second vignette)
questions.question: After a road traffic accident, a 37-year-old male was admitted to the emergency department; X-rays showed a fracture in the neck of the fibula. Which nerve may be affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The posterior tibial nerve runs deep in the posterior compartment, away from the subcutaneous fibular neck.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sciatic nerve has already divided proximal to the knee in most people, so only its common peroneal branch is at risk here, not the intact trunk.
explanations.C: Correct. "Lateral popliteal nerve" is this bank's older synonym for the common peroneal nerve, which winds directly around the fibular neck and is the nerve classically injured there. This older terminology names the nerve by the fossa it traverses (the lateral side of the popliteal fossa) rather than by its distal branching pattern, but it refers to the same common peroneal nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Medial popliteal nerve" is this bank's older synonym for the tibial nerve, which runs deep and posteromedial, away from the fibular neck.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise "lateral popliteal nerve" as this bank's synonym for the common peroneal nerve, injured at the fibular neck.

questions.title: Movement impaired by the same nerve injury
questions.question: As a result of this nerve injury, the patient may complain of severe impairment in:

options.D: Dorsi-flexion of foot and knee flexion

explanations.A: Incorrect. Plantarflexion is a tibial-nerve (posterior compartment) action, unaffected by a common peroneal nerve injury.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plantarflexion and inversion together are tibial-nerve actions, not common peroneal.
explanations.C: Correct. The common peroneal nerve drives the whole anterior compartment (dorsiflexors), so its injury produces severe dorsiflexion weakness — classic foot drop. Because plantarflexion and inversion (tibial-nerve actions) remain intact, the deficit is confined to the movements the anterior compartment alone produces.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Knee flexion is a hamstring (mostly tibial-division) action, largely spared by an isolated common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular neck.

questions.learning_objective: Link common peroneal nerve injury to dorsiflexion weakness (foot drop), sparing plantarflexion and knee flexion.

questions.title: Where the common peroneal nerve terminates
questions.question: The common peroneal nerve terminates inside ...... muscle.

explanations.A: Correct. The common peroneal nerve divides into its superficial and deep peroneal branches within the substance of peroneus longus, after winding around the fibular neck and piercing that muscle's origin. This detail matters clinically because a laceration or compression at peroneus longus itself, not only at the fibular neck, can produce the same distal nerve deficits.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Peroneus brevis lies distal to this division point and does not contain the nerve's bifurcation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Extensor digitorum longus is a deep-peroneal-nerve-supplied anterior compartment muscle, not the site of the common peroneal nerve's own division.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Popliteus is a tibial-nerve-supplied posterior compartment muscle, unrelated to the common peroneal nerve's course.

questions.learning_objective: State that the common peroneal nerve divides into its superficial/deep branches within peroneus longus.

questions.title: The false statement about the superficial peroneal nerve
questions.question: All of the following statements concerning the musculocutaneous nerve of the leg (superficial peroneal nerve) are true EXCEPT:

options.A: It supplies the peroneus longus muscle
options.B: It participates in the cutaneous supply of the dorsum of the foot
options.C: It passes deep to the extensor retinaculum of the foot
options.D: It is one of the 2 terminal branches of the common peroneal nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS true). The superficial peroneal nerve does supply peroneus longus (and brevis).
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS true). It does contribute most of the dorsum of the foot's cutaneous supply.
explanations.C: Correct — this is the false statement. The superficial peroneal nerve becomes cutaneous by piercing the deep fascia above the ankle and runs superficial to (not deep to) the extensor retinaculum; it is the deep peroneal nerve that passes deep to it. This distinction matters clinically: a superficial peroneal nerve injury near the ankle produces sensory loss over the dorsum without a foot-drop-type motor deficit, since the deep peroneal nerve (which does run deep to the retinaculum) is unaffected.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS true). It is one of the common peroneal nerve's two terminal branches, the other being the deep peroneal nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the superficial peroneal nerve's superficial course from the deep peroneal nerve's deep-to-retinaculum course.

questions.title: Muscle paralysed by a severed superficial peroneal nerve
questions.question: A motorcyclist falls from his bike and gets a deep gash that severs the superficial peroneal nerve near its origin. Which of the following muscles is paralyzed?

explanations.A: Correct. Peroneus longus, a lateral compartment muscle, is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve, so it is paralysed by this injury. Because peroneus brevis shares the same nerve, this injury also weakens eversion generally, not just the single named muscle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Extensor hallucis longus is deep-peroneal-nerve-supplied (anterior compartment), spared by a superficial peroneal nerve injury.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Extensor digitorum longus is likewise deep-peroneal-supplied, spared.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fibularis (peroneus) tertius is anatomically part of the anterior compartment and deep-peroneal-supplied despite its name, spared.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Extensor digitorum brevis, the one intrinsic dorsal foot muscle, is deep-peroneal-supplied, spared.

questions.learning_objective: Localise superficial peroneal nerve injury to peroneus longus/brevis paralysis, sparing the deep-peroneal-supplied muscles that share the "peroneus/fibularis" name pattern.
